description.narrative:
Insatsen avser stöd till Fas 2 av 2gether 4 SRHR som är ett regionalt FN-program som sedan 2018 genomförs av UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNICEF och WHO i östra och södra Afrika i syfte att stärka sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter (SRHR) genom att mer effektivt utnyttja de fyra deltagande FN-organens komparativa styrkor och tekniska expertis genom en koordinerad regional ansats. Programmets första fas 2018-2023 har finansierats av Sida med sammanlagt 568,7 MSEK. Programmets andra fas (2023-2027) bygger på resultat och lärdomar från den första fasen samt den externa utvärderingen av programmet (2022) med målet att påskynda uppnåendet av de SRHR-relaterade globala målen för hållbar utveckling i östra och södra Afrika med fokus på fyra förväntade övergripande resultat:
1.Den juridiska, politiska och finansiella miljön har stärkts för att möjliggöra tillgång till SRHR tjänster och förverkliga SRHR för alla med särskilt fokus på kvinnor, ungdomar, key populations och människor i krissituationer. 2.Ökad tillgång till och utnyttjande av högkvalitativa, individcentrerade integrerade SRHR-tjänster. 3.Sociala normer, könsnormer och drivkrafter för beteenden som främjar förverkligandet av SRHR för alla. 4.Motståndskraftiga hälso- och sjukvårdssystem och samhällen som kan säkerställa kontinuiteten i SRHR-tjänster i krissituation.
2gether4SRHR har en tydlig regional ansats med flexibla stödformer (finansieringsmekanismer och genomförandemetoder) för att kunna stödja strategiska SRHR-insatser i samtliga 23 länder i östra och södra Afrika. Insatsen har följande policymarkörer: Reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH), Gender equality, Democracy and Human Rights och Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR).

The contribution will support Phase 2 of 2gether4SRHR, which is a regional UN program implemented since 2018 by UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNICEF and WHO in Eastern and Southern Africa with the aim of strengthening sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) by more effectively leverage the comparative strengths and technical expertise of the four participating UN agencies through a coordinated regional approach. The program's first phase 2018-2023 has been financed by Sida with a total of SEK 568.7 million. The second phase of the program (2023-2027) builds on the results and lessons learned from the first phase and the external evaluation of the program (2022) with the aim of accelerating the achievement of the SRHR-related global goals for sustainable development in Eastern and Southern Africa with a focus on four expected overall results:
1. The legal, political and financial environment has been strengthened to enable access to SRHR services and realize SRHR for all with a particular focus on women, youth, key populations and people in crisis situations 2. Increased access to and utilization of high-quality, person-centered integrated SRHR services 3. Social norms, gender norms and behavioral drivers that promote the realization of SRHR for all 4. Resilient health systems and communities that can ensure the continuity of SRHR services in crisis situations.
2gether4SRHR has a clear regional approach with flexible forms of support (financing mechanisms and implementation methods) to be able to support strategic SRHR efforts in all 23 countries in eastern and southern Africa. The contribution has the following policy markers: Reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH), Gender equality, Democracy and Human Rights and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR).

The overall goal of the Programme is to contribute towards the attainment of the Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) related targets of SDGs 3 (good health and wellbeing) and 5 (gender equality) through four programme outcomes:
Outcome 1: Legal, policy and financial environment strengthened to enable beneficiaries to access services and realise their SRHR rights Output 1.1 - Political, legal and policy barriers reduced Output 1.2 - Domestic, bilateral and multilateral investment in SRHR increased
Outcome 2. Increased access to and utilisation of quality, people-centred integrated SRHR services Output 2.1 - Regional and national capacity to provide equitable access to quality integrated SRHR increased Output 2.2 Quality, people-centred integrated SRHR services scaled up Output 2.3 - High quality SRHR data and strategic information produced and used to inform the development of SRHR policies, funding and programme implementation
Outcome 3: Gender and social norms and behavioral drivers addressed for the realisation of SRHR for all Output 3.1 - Evidence on key gender norms, social norms, attitudes and values influencing SRHR outcomes used to enhance the development of SRHR policies, funding and programme implementation Output 3.2 Networks of regional adolescent & youth, key populations, and influential stakeholders, including religious and traditional leaders, engaged and empowered to promote positive gender and social norms in ESA
Outcome 4: Resilient health systems and communities are enabled to ensure the continuity of SRHR Services during crises Output 4.1 - Policy and legal environment enabled to address SRHR during humanitarian crisis and emergency situations Output 4.2 - Resilience of health systems strengthened to provide the minimum integrated SRHR service package (MISP) in times of crisis Output 4.3 - Evidence base for humanitarian and emergency response strengthened

description.narrative:
Some of the results in 2025 include:
Outcome 1: Legal, policy and financial environment strengthened to enable beneficiaries to access SRHR services and realise their SRHR rights
At the regional level, the program supported 7 regional frameworks and accountability instruments, strengthening regional harmonisation, policy coherence and normative guidance for the delivery of SRHR services. Key achievements that the program provided technical assistance to include the unanimous adoption of the SADC Key Populations HIV and SRHR Strategy, the update of SADC Minimum Standards for SRHR within Universal Health Coverage, the MidTerm Review of the SADC SRHR Strategy (20192030), and the finalization of the SADC Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning Plan for the SADC SRHR Scorecard.
The program also strengthened the integration of SRHR within universal health coverage and national health financing frameworks. A regional assessment of Essential Packages of Health Services across 13 countries identified gaps in SRHR inclusion and generated evidence based recommendations to support governments in expanding coverage of services.
Furthermore, the program gave support to SRHRUniversal Health Covergae sustainability roadmaps in Uganda, Tanzania, Lesotho, Namibia, and Zimbabwe in order to advance financing reforms by embedding SRHR priorities within HIV transition planning, domestic resource mobilisation strategies, and integrated service delivery models. The program introduced the Resource Allocation and Financial Tracking methodology, which improved countries' fiscal space analysis and strengthened the credibility of financing discussions with ministries of fifinance. Notable progress included Tanzanias introduction of a new HIV levy to safeguard integrated HIV and SRHR services, and Ugandas development of a costed roadmap demonstrating strong return on investment for sustained SRHR programming.
Outcome 2: Increased access to and utilisation of quality, people-centred integrated SRHR services
Strategic investments expanded Comprehensive Abortion Care programming and health systems integration. The continued collaboration with the UNFPA Supplies Partnership and Health Systems Strengthening funding stream ensured that Sweden's investment for unintended pregnancy and comprehensive abortion care programming in 2025 were complemented, thereby expanding access and policy interventions across 15 countries with a total joint investment of $830,866 comprising $550,000 from the UNFPA Supplies Partnership/HSS funding stream (10 Supplies countries) and $280,866 from 2gether 4 SRHR catalytic thematic funding (3 Non Supplies countries).
Innovative digital and service delivery models expanded access to integrated SRHR services, particularly in underserved communities. Namibia scaled-up mobile outreach services, reaching over 6,600 individuals with integrated SRHR, HIV, and GBV services, while Rwanda expanded access to comprehensive abortion care through a telehealth platform operating across 90 health centres. Botswana introduced virtual reality training and digital clinical decision support tools to strengthen healthcare worker competency and service quality.
Outcome 3: Gender and social norms, and behavioural drivers addressed
Youth-led networks significantly expanded their influence, with more than 250 young advocates engaging in high-level policy forums and securing institutionalised representation. The UNITED! Movement strengthened coordinated regional advocacy through its flagship campaign, expanded digital reach, and grew to over 700 members, while extensive capacity-building efforts equipped over 400 youth leaders and dozens of youth-led organizations with stronger governance, advocacy, and accountability skills.
Digital platforms supported by the program demonstrated substantial reach, including tens of thousands of users engaged through edutainment and online campaigns. At these platforms, the program reinforced the importance of linking awareness to structured referral systems to ensure behavioural impact.
Outcome 4: Ensuring resilient health systems and communities for continuous SRHR services during crises
Fifteen countries integrated SRH in Emergencies and Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) standards into their national disaster preparedness plans. In addition, 17 countries incorporated SRHR commitments into their Nationally Determined Contributions or National Adaptation Plans, marking a substantial structural shift linking SRHR to climate resilience.
The operationalisation of the program's standard operating procedures for the regional emergency fund enabled rapid disbursement to support refugee contexts. The surge capacity was strengthened through expansion of the SADC Humanitarian Response Centre to have a larger pool of humanitarian responders. This also included certification of additional regional MISP trainers, prepositioning of emergency supplies and commodities, and training of frontline workers and community agents.
